analytic.title: The Hyperbolic Schedulability Bound for Multiprocessor RM Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: To verify the feasibility of real-time task sets on homogeneous multiprocessor systems, Lopez et al. derived the utilization bound based on Best Fit Decreasing allocation algorithm and Rate-Monotonic scheduling, which coincides with the maximum achievable multiprocessor utilization bound, using Liu & Lyland bound as the uniprocessor schedulability condition. In this paper, a novel feasibility test for the same target problem is developed based on the hyperbolic bound due to Bini et al., instead of the Liu & Layland bound. Analytical and experimental results show that the proposed utilization bound performs better than the existing bound under quite a lot of parameter settings, and combining these two bounds together can significantly increase the number of schedulable task sets with little extra overhead.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Multiprocessor scheduling, a challenging problem in realtime scheduling, has drawn much attention from the realtime research community lately due to the advent of multicore architectures. Two main strategies, namely, the partitioning strategy and the global strategy, have been investigated to schedule real-time tasks on a multiprocessor platform. Although the former may provide higher schedulability than the latter in theory, the partitioning strategy, in which each and every task must be always executed on the same processor once assigned, seems much more appealing in practice due to its simplicity and low scheduling overhead.

A specific partitioning strategy is determined by the <allocation algorithm, uniprocessor scheduling algorithm> pair. In [1], the multiprocessor utilization bound U RM -BF D LLB , given in Inequality (1) below, was derived to establish the schedulability condition of real-time task sets under Best Fit Decreasing (BFD) allocation algorithm and Rate-Monotonic (RM) scheduling algorithm, where u i is the utilization factor of task i, and n and m denote the number of processors and the number of tasks, respectively. The parameter β will be discussed later in Section II. In the calculation of U RM -BF D LLB , Liu & Lyland bound (LLB), given by Equation (3) in Section 2, is used as the uniprocessor schedulability condition. U RM -BF D LLB was shown to achieve the maximum bound possible among all reasonable allocation algorithms for RM scheduling using LLB [1].

The hyperbolic bound (HB), given by Equation ( 5) in Section 2, is a novel uniprocessor schedulability analysis technique proposed by Bini et al, which offers better performance than LLB in that more tasks sets can be accepted by HB [2]. Specifically, a task set that is schedulable under LLB can always pass the schedulability test with HB, but the reverse is not necessarily true. The HB-based schedulability test has the same complexity O(m) as the LLB-based one. While many experimental studies confirm that using HB as the uniprocessor schedualbility condition on multiprocessors can increase the number of schedulable real-time task sets significantly [3], [4], to the best of our knowledge, no theoretical result has been developed with respect to HBbased multiprocessor utilization bounds.

With the increasing prevalence of multicore and multiprocessor systems, a theoretical treatment of the aforementioned problem is imperative. In this paper, we study the problem of scheduling real-time tasks on multiprocessors under BFD allocation and RM scheduling. Different from the work in [1], [5], we use the hyperbolic bound as the uniprocessor schedulability condition, and derive a novel utilization bound U RM -BF D HB , which is given in Equation (2) and will be discussed in detail in Section 3.

div.head: II. PRELIMINARIES
div.p: In this section, we shall formally define the system model used throughout this paper. We consider a homogeneous n processor platform
div.formula: {P 1 , P 2 , • • • , P n }, on which a set of m individual periodic tasks {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ m } execute.
div.p: Each task τ i is characterized by its computation time C i , period T i and relative deadline D i . We assume that task deadlines are hard and equal to the task periods (D i = T i ). The utilization u i of any task τ i , defined as C i /T i , is assumed to be 0 < u i ≤ α ≤ 1, where α is the maximum utilization factor over all tasks.

Tasks are allocated to n processors {P 1 , P 2 , • • • , P n } according to Best Fit Deceasing allocation algorithm. With BFD, tasks are first ordered by decreasing utilization factors before making the allocation, i.e,

Based on this ordering, the BFD heuristic allocates each task to the processor with the lowest remaining capacity among those with enough remaining capacity to hold the task. That is, the task is allocated to the processor in which it fits best [7]. Once a task is allocated to a processor it executes only on that processor. Within each processor, tasks are pre-emptively scheduled based on fixed priorities that are assigned according to the RM order.
Utilization-bound-based feasibility test was first introduced by Liu & Layland for uniprocessor RM scheduling [8], which is given by Equation(3):

LLB is only sufficient in the sense that task sets with utilization greater than m(2 1/m -1) could be still schedulable under RM scheduling. A sufficient and necessary schedulability condition was obtained by Lehoczky et al. [9], yet it is too complex to be adopted in deriving a multiprocessor utilization bound. Thus, in [1], LLB was adopted as the uniprocessor schedulability condition in the calculation of U RM -BF D LLB . The parameter β in Equation ( 1) is defined as the maximum number of tasks of utilization factor α that can fit into one processor using LLB for RM scheduling. β can be expressed as a function of α as follows [1]:

To test the feasibility of large task sets more effectively, a better schedulability analysis method, the hyperbolic bound, was proposed by Bini et al. in [2]. HB has provable better performance than LLB and is also the best possible bound that can be found by the mere knowledge of task utilization factors. With HB, a set of m tasks is schedulable if Equation( 5) is satisfied.

To simplify discussion, we refer to the product of (u i +1)s of a set of tasks as HB-utilization in the rest of this paper. With HB, a task of utilization factor u k fits into processor P j , which already has m j tasks allocated to it with total HB-utilization

div.p: On multiprocessors of size n, if the aforementioned equation does not hold for all 1 ≤ j ≤ n, BFD will fail to allocate this task and the task set is said to be unschedulable using HB.

The Reasonable Allocation Decreasing (RAD) algorithms are a class of allocation algorithms fulfilling (1) task are ordered by decreasing utilizations factors before making the allocation; (2) tasks are allocated sequentially and the allocation algorithm fails only if there is no processor having sufficient capacity to hold the pending task. div.head: IV. THE EXPERIMENTS
div.p: To evaluate the performance of a feasibility test, one method is to analytically compute the acceptance ratio, i.e., the fraction of task sets that pass the test with respect to the total number of feasible ones. However, as pointed out in [10], computing the acceptance ratio using a rigorous approach is not always possible, except for very simple cases. Alternatively, the performance of a feasibility test is often evaluated through extensive simulations, where a huge number of synthetic task sets need to be generated. In view of the difficulty in computing the acceptance ratio theoretically for either U RM -BF D HB or U RM -BF D LLB , we experimentally evaluate the performance of U RM -BF D HB , in comparison with U RM -BF D LLB , under a large variety of parameter settings. Our experimental methodology is similar to the one adopted in [11]. The task utilizations are chosen according to the following distributions:
1. uniform distribution between (0, 2 1/γ -1), γ = 1, 2, . . . , 20.
2. bimodel distribution: heavy tasks uniform between (0.5, 1) and light tasks uniform between (0,0.5), probability of being heavy = 0.25, 0.33, 0.67 and 0.75.
3. exponential distribution with mean 0.1, 0.25, 0.5.

We do not simulate task periods and computation times explicitly because the two feasibility tests are only affected by task utilization. Datasets are generated for 4, 8, 12 and 16 processor systems as follows. Initially, 1,000,000 task sets, each of which consisting of n tasks, are generated according to the given utilization distribution. Then for each task set, one new task is generated and added in, and both feasibility tests are carried out on the new task set. For a single task set, the procedure of adding new tasks is repeated until the total utilization exceeds n. The whole procedure ends if the utilization of every of the 1,000,000 task sets is greater than n.

The main performance measure is the Success Ratio, which is defined as the proportion of generated task sets that can pass the LLB-based test (HB-based test). To gain a detailed insight into the performance of both bounds, we divide the full range of total utilizations possible into intervals of size 0.1. The statistics are collected for each interval. Besides, the total number of feasible task sets using HB (denoted by Num(HB-M)), the total number of feasible task sets using LLB (denoted by Num(LLB-M)), the number of task sets that are feasible using HB and infeasible using LLB, and the number of task sets that are infeasible using HB and feasible using LLB are also collected.

div.head: A. Experiment Results
div.p: As similar patterns are exhibited across all parameter settings that we have experimented with, only partial results are reported in this section. Figure 1 to Figure 8 show the experimental results for the uniform utilization distribution, where HB-M and LLB-M stand for U RM -BF D HB and U RM -BF D LLB , respectively. As shown in these figures, HB-M is always superior to LLB-M in the case of small values of γ (=1,2). As γ increases, the performance of HB-M degrades gradually, and eventually becomes worse than that of LLB-M in terms of the total number of feasible task sets. It has been proved in [2] that LLB and HB are equivalent on uniprocessors when the utilizations of all tasks are equal. Together with Observation 2, we know that the ratio between the number of feasible task sets using HB-M and the number of feasible task sets using LLB-M converges to 1 as γ approaches infinity, which is borne out by results shown in Figure 11.

Figure 9, 10, 12 and 13 are for task sets of the bimodel utilization distribution. As shown in these figures, with the reduction in the probability of being a light task, the gain of HB-M with respect to LLB-M decreases gradually, which indicates that HB-M is more favored when the population of large utilization tasks is dominant. Once again, these results confirm our observation that HB-M performs better in the case of large variance of utilization factors.

The experimental results for the exponential distribution are depicted in Figure 14 to Figure 16. As we can see, HB-M surpasses LLB-M in most cases when the mean value is equal to 0.5. As the mean value decreases, the performance of HB-M begins to degrade, and eventually HB-M is outperformed by LLB-M. Two reasons account for this phenomenon. Firstly, the utilizations of most tasks are small in the case of small mean values, which leads to the increase in m i=1 (u i + 1). Secondly, HB-M (2 nγ+1 γ+1 ) has much chance to be minimized with respect to γ because large utilization tasks may still be generated even if the mean values are small. Please note that it is impossible for these two cases to occur simultaneously in the uniform distribution.

div.head: B. Compatibility of Both Bounds
div.p: The experimental results discussed in Section 4.1 indicate that neither HB-M nor LLB-M outperforms the other across all parameter settings. According to the taxonomy in [6], HB-M and LLB-M are incomparable in that none of them is superior to the other completely. Fortunately, both feasibility tests (HB-M and LLB-M) are based on RM scheduling and BFD, and therefore compatible with each other. To be specific, as long as a task set passes either HB-M or LLB-M test, it can be scheduled successfully using RM and BFD on multiprocessors. It is worth noting that such a combined feasibility test does not incur much extra overhead because it keeps the O(m) complexity of schedulability test unchanged.

Figure 17 to Figure 19 show that the combined use of HB-M and LLB-M improves the overall performance significantly compared with the separate use of LLB-M. for given scheduling algorithms, so that one can quickly evaluate the feasibility of a specific task set. For our study, we only focus on partitioning-based fixed-priority multiprocessor scheduling. We refer interested readers to [6] for a more complete discussion of other research topics on multiprocessor real-time scheduling.

Most of the early research into partitioning-based staticpriority multiprocessor scheduling centered on the design and analysis of novel allocation algorithms, by which tasks are partitioned into groups and then assigned to different processors [12], [13], [14]. In 1998, Oh and Baker derived the utilization bound based on RM scheduling and the First Fit heuristic. It was proved that RM-FF meets all task deadlines if less than 41% of the processor capacity is requested [5].

In 2001, B. Andersson et al. showed that with respect to the partitioning strategy, the utilization bound for any allocation algorithm is less than (n + 1)/2 [15]. Two years later, they proposed an allocation algorithm, ROUND-MP-NFR, that renders a utilization bound of n/2. This result demonstrates that a task partitioning algorithm, which can almost achieve maximum possible utilization bound, does exist.

Lopez et al. generalized the result in [5] by taking maximum task utilization and number of tasks to be scheduled into consideration. A series of utilization bounds had been provided for RM-FF, RM-BFD , RM-FFD and RM-WF, which have better performance than the aforementioned bounds when the maximum task utilization is relatively small.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper a novel feasibility test is developed for RM scheduling and BFD allocation algorithm on multiprocessors using the hyperbolic bound. We have conducted extensive simulation experiments, which show that the proposed hyperbolic bound and the traditional one can only do well in some parameter setting, respectively. Thanks to the compatibility of these two tests, we can achieve up to 3.4 times more feasible task sets by the combined feasibility test compared with separate use of either one.
